entry.title: Local Work, Global Progress: A Convergence Theory of AI Agent Collaboration
entry.summary: Teams of large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to complex tasks, but their collaboration protocols are mostly designed empirically, without convergence guarantees. We formalize collaborative problem solving as block optimization: each agent improves one part of a shared solution, guided by its local objective plus a correction for how its changes affect the other parts. A coordinator checks every proposal against the global objective and merges proposals that do not interfere with each other. We prove linear convergence up to an error floor that vanishes when the corrections are exact. Interfering proposals can also be merged once their combination has been checked; the rate then depends on how well the proposals actually combine, not on worst-case interactions. With GPT-OSS-120B agents on robot routing, a three-agent team finds collision-free plans in every run, better than those of a single agent that controls all robots. On a larger routing task, a six-agent team completes its search about twice as fast as the single agent (in median). Merging the best checked combination of proposals, rather than only proposals that do not interfere, cuts the team's search time by about 30%. With constants measured on the runs, our convergence bound holds in every round and follows the observed progress. We also test the theory on query planning in SQLite and on a synthetic task.

entry.title: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with 500 Million Household Persona Agents
entry.summary: Simulating economic responses at society scale requires agents whose decisions reflect household circumstances and the effects of earlier actions. We introduce S$^2$-MAS, a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework built on 500 million synthetic household personas grounded in real-survey data. Its Genese engine separates decisions from state updates, while reusable financial scenarios and application ledgers track consumption, cash, debt and payments. FinL-mlx, a compact decision model trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question-macro F1 in consumer financial-choice scenarios, outperforming Jev 1.13 and GLM-5.3-Flash on both measures. We evaluate eight financial task families and simulate 12 million distinct household agents in paired purchase-funding conditions. Jointly raising purchase goals and approved credit limits increases consumption, with responses differing across age and income groups. Education, employment and household-size differences persist after age--income standardization and mainly reflect transitions from deferral to purchase. Asset and debt groups differ in cash drawdown, repayment and closing debt. A 24-month panel varies purchase goals under a common credit product, with repayment and arrears updating subsequent offers. S$^2$-MAS links heterogeneous household decisions to evolving consumption, cash and repayment paths, supporting economic experiments across household groups, population scales and time horizons.

Publication: 58 pages, 13 main figures, 7 supplementary figures

entry.title: Complete Street Design informed by Multi-Agent Simulation
entry.summary: Objectives: Complete Street design is currently guided largely by qualitative principles despite the increasing complexity of multimodal urban traffic. This paper develops a microscopic simulation framework for quantitatively evaluating alternative street designs by explicitly representing heterogeneous road users, including Autonomous Vehicles (AVs), Connected Vehicles (CVs), Human-Driven Vehicles (HDVs), pick-up and drop-off (PUDO) services, and micromobility users. The framework jointly evaluates mobility and safety within a unified testbed. Methods:The framework enriches microscopic simulation with behavioral models for heterogeneous road users. It explicitly captures lateral movements, parking maneuvers, pedestrian crossings and jaywalking, and shared-lane bicycle and scooter interactions. Safety is quantified using a conflict severity measure grounded in collision physics, while candidate street layouts are optimized using a genetic algorithm. Findings: Applied to a segment of Belmont Avenue in Chicago, Illinois, the framework shows that dedicated bicycle lanes reduce conflict severity at the expense of vehicular throughput. Increasing AV penetration mitigates congestion by reducing traffic shockwaves while improving interactions with pedestrians relative to CVs and HDVs. The optimization framework efficiently identifies Pareto-efficient street layouts that balance mobility and safety. Novelty: The proposed framework integrates heterogeneous behavioral modeling, physics-based conflict assessment, stochastic performance evaluation, and design optimization within a single quantitative framework for Complete Street design. Practical Applications: The framework provides transportation planners with a predictive virtual testbed for evaluating street designs and quantifying the tradeoff between mobility and safety before implementation.
entry.content:
Publication: Under review for publication in Transportation Research Record (TRR)

Category: Method

entry.title: Discovery-Probability Graph Planning for Embodied Agents in Tasks with Hidden Cooperation Requirements
entry.summary: Embodied agents are increasingly capable of perceiving, planning, and acting autonomously in dynamic environments, demonstrating strong performance on complex cooperative tasks. Recent advances typically assume that cooperative tasks are known in advance. In real-world applications, however, hidden-cooperation tasks are more common: the need for cooperation only becomes apparent after an agent observes and interacts with task-related targets. In this paper, we first present HiddenCoop, a benchmark for effectively evaluating agent cooperation in hidden-cooperation tasks. We further propose Discovery-Probability Graph Planning (DPGP), a method for enabling effective agent cooperation in such tasks. At the core of DPGP is a discovery-probability graph that encodes the probability distribution over the number and locations of task-related targets, facilitating effective and efficient information exchange among agents. A search algorithm is then used to derive action plans that minimize expected costs. Experiments show that DPGP achieves cooperative-task success rates of 99.3% on C-WAH and 58.3% on TDW-MAT, surpassing all compared baselines, while also reducing overall embodied execution time and substantially lowering LLM token usage. Our code is available at https://github.com/hnu-vis/DPGP.

entry.title: Behavioral Probes for Information Flow in LLM Swarms
entry.summary: Most existing approaches to LLM swarm optimization are utility-driven, focusing on final task utility while leaving the processing, integration, and reliance of information within individual interactions largely implicit. To address this, we study LLM swarm interactions from an information-flow-based view and introduce behavioral probes to quantify information flow patterns. Specifically, we repurpose External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS)---originally designed for hallucination analysis---to measure a node's external-context dependence and parametric-knowledge dependence, respectively. Across controlled and realistic swarm settings, we observe consistent patterns: ECS increases with input relevance and distinguishes useful multi-source contributions, while PKS decreases as informative context accumulates. Building on this heuristic interpretation, we demonstrate how these probes can complement utility-driven structure optimization in two controlled applications. Probe-guided node pruning reduces redundant communication and token consumption, and probe-guided reasoning-path search accelerates convergence compared to utility-only baselines. Our empirical results suggest that behavioral probes can make the internal information flow of LLM swarms observable and serve as effective auxiliary signals for structure optimization.

entry.title: Learning Who Talks to Whom: Role-Aware Communication Topology Scheduling for Efficient LLM Multi-Agent Collaboration
entry.summary: Multi-agent systems driven by large language models (LLMs) rely on structured communication topologies to facilitate information exchange and collaborative reasoning. However, effectively scheduling these topologies to dynamically determine who talks to whom and when to communicate remains a fundamental challenge in balancing collective reasoning performance against exponential token overhead. Existing topology scheduling approaches either enforce static communication graphs that cannot adapt to dynamic problem-solving states, or overlook agent role complementarity while failing to explicitly incorporate the synthesized graph structure into team-level decision evaluation. To tackle these limitations, we propose ACTS, a role-aware adaptive communication topology scheduling framework for efficient LLM multi-agent collaboration. Orchestrated within a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm, ACTS introduces a novel dual-attention mechanism. Specifically, a Role-conditioned Relational Attention module dynamically selects variable-cardinality interaction partners based on agent roles and evolving execution states, while a Topological Attention Mixer explicitly embeds the directed communication topology into team value decomposition for precise credit assignment. Comprehensive evaluations across 9 challenging benchmarks covering code generation, multi-step reasoning, general knowledge, and competitive mathematics demonstrate that ACTS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, boosting average accuracy by up to 6.19 percentage points while reducing token consumption by over 15%. The project website is available at https://acts-mas.github.io/ACTS/.

entry.title: How Far Can an Agent Push? Trust-Safety Margins in Live Language-Based Economic Games
entry.summary: The previous version contained Unicode em dashes. Paste this ASCII-only version: Game theory identifies when a strategic action should be accepted, but not how long a live, language-based counterpart will continue to accept it. We entered the GLEE competition in its final week with one protected agent, Milton, and four instrument agents that ran deterministic, per-game randomized trials of policy changes; Milton received changes only through pre-specified gates or registered, rollback-guarded production rules. In negotiation, learned pricing improves adjusted percentile by 0.071 (n=21,168); in bargaining, a continuation model conditioned on the rejected offer did not improve on a recency-weighted incumbent and was retired. In persuasion, a preregistered five-dose experiment (7,391 assigned games, blinded until a fixed stop) shows that recommending every unit raises sales by 0.194 of the maximum (95% CI [0.147, 0.241]) where the receiver's slack makes obedience rational (52% of the Bayesian benchmark), lowers them where it does not (-0.067), and produces a larger early-to-late purchase decline than honest recommendations (-0.123). A rule fixed before unblinding now routes Milton's dose per cell. Milton stood 11th of 460 agents in bargaining at the fixed stop; we also report the close, where the final day's pool shift moved all five agents' bargaining ratings together while their play was unchanged, and three dispatch defects were found by checking delivered behavior against the design.

entry.title: AgentSoV: Virtual Sensing for LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Stream of Variation
entry.summary: Large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems (MASs) solve complex tasks through interacting agents, yet their reliability is difficult to analyze because failures depend on both individual agents and how information and errors propagate across the system. Existing approaches largely treat this as post-hoc failure attribution, but do not provide a common model across heterogeneous MAS architectures or support broader analysis of information influence and observability. We introduce AgentSoV, a virtual-sensing framework that models MAS execution as a stochastic dynamic system through Stream of Variation (SoV). AgentSoV maps heterogeneous trajectories into diagnostic stages, constructs virtual measurements from observable outputs, and learns cross-stage variation propagation with a state-space model. Its representation is architecture-aware in stage dependencies yet architecture-agnostic in analytical language, supporting chain-structured, orchestration-based, and directed acyclic graph (DAG)-structured MASs. Without re-executing the MAS, AgentSoV supports three system-level analyses: failure attribution identifies where abnormal variation enters; stage-input influence quantifies how strongly intermediate inputs affect downstream outcomes; and virtual-sensor placement selects complementary observations under a monitoring budget. Experiments across multiple MAS architectures demonstrate a unified approach to fault localization, information influence, and observability. AgentSoV reframes agentic execution as a dynamic system to model rather than merely text to inspect, providing insights for MAS structure and component design.

entry.title: Measuring Consensus in AI Agent Networks
entry.summary: As AI agents become increasingly connected through networks and take on tasks that require negotiation and joint decision-making, a systematic approach is needed to assess how their views converge and what information supports their decisions. We present an evaluation framework that treats consensus formation as the evolution of publicly stated positions toward a shared region, using accumulated communication history as context. The framework tracks position trajectories, group dispersion, and information expressed in public messages. Two case studies examine staffing decisions based on distributed facts and decisions requiring agents to reconcile duplicate information and a cancelled contract. Results from 1,872 completed runs associate sharing explanations with more accurate group decisions, while the second task reveals persistent disagreement despite accurate aggregate answers. Membership-change experiments provide a complementary evaluation. By separating convergence among agents from progress toward a task's full-information answer, the framework relates decision accuracy and bounded disagreement to the information available during the exchange.

entry.title: CARVS: A Congestion-Aware Algorithm for Online Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery in Human-Collaborative Warehouses
entry.summary: Intelligent warehouse systems have transformed logistics by integrating robots with minimal infrastructure changes, boosting efficiency and optimizing workflows compared to traditional human-only operations. However, human-robot collaboration introduces new challenges, particularly due to human uncertainty, which leads to dynamic interactions and unpredictable behavior. To address these complexities, this paper presents the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery with Human Collaboration (MAPDwHC) problem, an extension of the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery (MAPD) problem that incorporates human unpredictability. This problem adds key constraints, such as dynamic obstacles caused by robots temporarily blocking paths when interacting with humans, and the need for real-time responsiveness. We formalize the MAPDwHC problem with additional constraints and properties. Based on this problem setting, we propose the CARVS algorithm, which improves task assignment and path planning by integrating task swapping, validation checks, and random initialization. CARVS reduces congestion, enhances adaptability to human-robot interactions, and ensures real-time responsiveness. Simulation results show that CARVS significantly reduces timeouts of path planning in large-scale scenarios where traditional MAPD algorithms fail, improving both efficiency and scalability.

entry.title: Towards High Semantic Fidelity: Hyperdimensional Symbolic Messages in Multi-Agent Communication
entry.summary: Semantic fidelity is essential for multi-agent communication under non-ideal channels, comprising transmission fidelity and conversion fidelity. Yet existing numerical and neural message formats cannot simultaneously achieve both. To address this, we propose a novel message format-\textbf{H}yperdimensional \textbf{S}ymbolic \textbf{M}essages (HSM) and its corresponding communication framework \textbf{Herm}. For transmission fidelity, Herm suppresses semantic entanglement via an entity-attribute-value structured encoding pipeline. For conversion fidelity, Herm first leverages a receiver-centric ego-binding mechanism to align semantics. Then, a similarity-aware dual-branch fusion module is proposed to prevent critical semantic dilution. To realize explicit message-semantic conversion, we devise an iterative decoding scheme via algebraic inverse operations. Experiments exhibit that Herm outperforms baselines across various noisy scenarios while maintaining superior structural readability.

entry.title: Thought Blocks: Non-Autoregressive Latent Communication for Multi-Agent Systems via Trajectory-to-State Compilation
entry.summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems typically communicate through text, incurring repeated generation and re-encoding costs. Although latent communication removes explicit verbalization, constructing latent messages may still require autoregressive latent trajectories. We therefore distinguish message representation from message construction and ask whether agents can directly construct useful continuation states without executing the trajectories that normally produce them. We formulate this problem as trajectory-to-state compilation and introduce Thought Blocks, fixed-size blocks of latent key--value (KV) continuation memory constructed in one shot. Thought Blocks achieve a 2.5 times average latency speedup over autoregressive latent communication. Compared with text-based multi-agent communication, Thought Blocks reduce text tokens by 45.7% and autoregressive steps by 84.8%, achieving an 8.6 times average latency speedup. These results demonstrate that trajectory-to-state compilation enables efficient inter-agent latent communication without sequential latent rollouts at inference.

entry.title: ROAR: Benchmarking LMM Agents under Real-Time Constraints in Multiplayer Action-Shooter Games
entry.summary: Large multimodal models (LMMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that perceive, reason, and act in interactive multi-agent environments. Yet most existing benchmarks for LMM-based agents in multi-agent settings remain turn-based: the environment and other agents pause while an agent performs inference. Such protocols obscure a fundamental challenge of real-time constraints, where the world continues to evolve and delayed decisions may become outdated before execution. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce ROAR, a multiplayer action-shooter game environment for evaluating LMM-based agents in multi-agent settings under real-time constraints. ROAR covers cooperative, competitive, mixed cooperative-competitive, and basic single-agent scenarios. We further propose a Multi-Agent Asynchronous Gym interface that decouples environment evolution from agent reasoning by running the environment and each agent in separate threads, enabling the environment to advance at fixed time intervals without waiting for LMM inference and allowing agents to reason independently without blocking one another. ROAR also features convenient deployment, multimodal observations, and customizable levels. ROAR offers a practical testbed for advancing LMM-based agents beyond static, turn-based evaluation toward real-time multi-agent decision-making.

entry.title: Model Capacity Frontier: A Development Framework for LLM-Supported Social Simulation
entry.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. Developing LLM-supported ABMs to simulate human collective behavior therefore requires navigating configuration sensitivity while identifying the limitations of the current model architecture. In this paper, we introduce the \textit{Model Capacity Frontier} (MCF), a framework that characterizes the empirical performance attainable by a specified architecture across its admissible configurations. In multi-objective settings, this capacity is represented by an estimated Pareto frontier obtained through systematic configuration exploration. We demonstrate MCF in crowd simulation of university commencement events with approximately 12,000 agents, using empirical movement data on temporal occupancy, spatial distribution, and flow direction. We first characterize the capacity of a conventional crowd model and then evaluate successive LLM-supported architectural extensions. In the process, MCF reveals which dimensions of attainable performance expand and which remain limited, providing empirical targets for refinement and re-evaluation. Initial LLM integration improves flow direction but degrades temporal occupancy and spatial distribution; subsequent architectural refinement of the LLM layer improves temporal occupancy and recovers spatial performance, while retaining much of the earlier gain in flow direction. Our case study shows how MCF guides the systematic architectural development of LLM-supported ABMs in configuration-sensitive, open-ended design spaces.

entry.title: The Weight of Teamwork: Does Communication Structure Help LLM Scientists Search for Scientific Laws?
entry.summary: Team performance is often reported as one delivered score, even though that score is produced in two stages: a system generates candidate answers and a selection rule returns one of them. We use symbolic regression as an observable scientific-search setting and compare fixed-budget LLM teams that differ in peer visibility and update timing, evaluating both their frozen candidate archives and the expressions selected from those archives. Distributing the call budget across more independent trajectories produced the largest measured gain, improving mean held-out fitting score Q by 0.70 at the widest tested allocation. Under a common archive-wide selector, the implemented Ring policy reduced mean Q by 0.33 relative to Independent, while Star and Complete remained unresolved. Holding the generated archives fixed, changing the delivery rule changed the measured architecture gaps, including the sign of the Complete point estimate. These results support reporting candidate generation and final selection as separate endpoints. They do not identify a communication mechanism or a universally preferred topology; rather, they show that an architecture ranking is not identified by communication structure alone when the rule that returns the final answer is left unspecified.
entry.content:
Publication: the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundations of Agentic Systems Theory (FAST)

Category: Method

entry.title: LLM Evolution in a Simple Simulated Market
entry.summary: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.

entry.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
entry.summary: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.

entry.title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines
entry.summary: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.

entry.title: Agentic-Priors: Using Large Language Models to Address the Cold Start Problem in Preference Elicitation
entry.summary: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.

entry.title: MetaShare: Failure-Aware Collective Self-Improvement for Open-Ended Agents
entry.summary: Humans often learn fastest not by repeating success, but by remembering which failures not to repeat. Open-ended self-improving agents can share experience across lineages, as in GEA, or edit their own improvement mechanisms, as in DGM-Hyperagents, yet failed improvement attempts are rarely retained as reusable cross-branch knowledge, and search can collapse onto redundant strategies. We introduce MetaShare, a failure-aware framework that records successful and unsuccessful agent modifications together with signed performance deltas. Before each generation, MetaShare retrieves diverse high-performing strategies alongside high-confidence failures from other lineages, letting agents reuse effective mechanisms while avoiding known dead ends. A task-blind auditor periodically injects absent or underrepresented mechanism categories, while embedding-based de-ranking limits redundancy during retrieval. Multiple meta-agents propose modifications in parallel at heterogeneous temperatures behind a deterministic selector that gates applicability, scope, compilability, and size. Experiments across paper review, coding, math grading, robotics reward design, and financial audit-risk assessment show that MetaShare's median matches or exceeds DGM-Hyperagents' final performance and reaches its own best-performing agent in 1.7--2.9$\times$ fewer evolution iterations.
entry.content:
Publication: NeurIPS 2026 Meta-Agents Workshop (Managing Agents that Manage Agents)

Category: Method

entry.title: The Delegation Dilemma: Economies of Scale, Accountability, and Polycentric Governance
entry.summary: Many collective-action systems are neither fully decentralized nor fully centralized: agents voluntarily organize into institutions that share organizational costs and delegate decisions to representatives. Delegation can reduce individual costs, but it also transfers control to representatives whose private objectives need not align with those of their constituents. We study this tension in a repeated game with endogenous delegation to self-interested centers. A simple reduced-form model yields a scale--accountability tradeoff: larger constituencies offer greater cost-sharing benefits to members, yet the marginal value to a center of retaining any one constituent decreases as group size grows. Consequently, the prospect of individual exit can sustain non-exploitative delegation only up to an endogenous accountable constituency size. Additionally, we identify parameter regions in which fully delegated, accountable governance, when feasible, must be polycentric. We investigate these predictions through simulations with large language model (LLM) agents. Across five matched pairs of 30-agent simulations, polycentric structures repeatedly emerge but remain fluid, exhibiting cycles of concentration, exploitation, exit, and re-formation. We further find that models of different capacity exhibit similar willingness to assume leadership but differ substantially in their exercise of authority, with Sol initiating exploitation more frequently than Luna in matched decision states.

entry.title: A Responsibility-Centered Coordination Mechanism for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems
entry.summary: Centralized orchestration provides comprehensive multi-agent coordination but creates bottlenecks in scalability, adaptability, and collective performance. Decentralized approaches alleviate these bottlenecks by distributing coordination across agents, yet often leave responsibility for delegated dependencies and failure recovery unclear. To address this gap, we propose RCM, a responsibility-centered coordination mechanism that leverages commitments to couple task delegation with explicit responsibilities of the involved parties. Through recursive delegation, agents retain their upstream responsibilities while locally orchestrating downstream commitments, thereby preserving accountability across delegation chains, creating a network of local orchestration. We operationalize this mechanism locally through responsibility-constrained decision-making and a responsibility-oriented communication protocol (RCP), enabling agents to autonomously establish, manage, and terminate commitments. As agents act in parallel, their local actions continuously evolve the commitment graph, allowing global coordination to emerge and adapt toward a shared mission without centralized control. Experiments across reasoning, coding, and executable agent environments demonstrate that RCM outperforms strong centralized and decentralized coordination baselines by up to 18.7 points in task performance and 10.2 points in Responsibility, while improving failure and harm detection without task-specific training.

entry.title: SSR: Structural Signal Retriever for Scalable Agent Discovery in LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Agent Systems
entry.summary: Large-scale multi-agent ecosystems require mechanisms for discovering suitable agents without exposing entire registries to a large language model (LLM) orchestrator. The challenge is not only to retrieve relevant Agent Cards from a growing registry, but also to maintain a compact candidate context, since each additional candidate increases prompt size, inference cost, latency, and the risk of exceeding the model context window. We formulate this problem as candidate-context scalability and propose the Structural Signal Retriever (SSR), our deterministic and training-free retrieval method designed for Agent Card discovery. SSR derives structural lexical signals from capability-bearing Agent Card fields, weights them using inverse document frequency (IDF), and uses an Inverted Signal Index (ISI) for selective candidate scoring. We evaluate SSR using a synthetic agent benchmark, a public MS MARCO adaptation, and end-to-end LLM orchestration. At 1,000 agents, SSR reduces LLM input by 98.8% and orchestration latency by 70.9% relative to full-catalog orchestration. On MS MARCO, IDF improves retrieval effectiveness within the structural representation, while the ISI preserves retrieval effectiveness and reduces explicitly scored passages by 96.8%. End-to-end experiments show that candidate pre-selection maintains a compact candidate context as registry size grows and avoids the operational failures observed with full-catalog orchestration. These results support SSR as an Agent-Card-native, traceable retrieval mechanism for candidate-context scalability.

entry.title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
entry.summary: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks. We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource. This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests. We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes foregoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements. We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings. Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or lightweight models. Alongside cooperation, we observe exclusionary coalitions and rare divide-and-conquer strategies. SCARCE provides a controlled setting for proactively and systematically auditing how these relationships emerge, shape access to resources, and affect the safety and coordination of multi-agent systems.

entry.title: Emergent Discrimination and Polarization in Multi-Agent Systems
entry.summary: We study theoretically how discrimination and polarization can emerge in a population of learning agents. Each agent uses an adaptive linear decision layer to map a language-model embedding of an issue to a binary opinion and maintains an evolving estimate of how much it trusts every other agent. Through pairwise interactions, agents update both their decision weights and trust estimates using an online Bayesian rule derived from teacher-student learning over a noisy channel. In-context-learning experiments with large language models qualitatively reproduce the predicted opinion and trust updates. We then assign each agent one of two arbitrary group labels, A or B, and model group bias by allowing a fraction $f_b$ of agents to shift its perceived agreement with each message by a strength $b$, a bias steering prejudice, depending on whether the sender and receiver share a label. We use order parameters from statistical mechanics to connect these local dynamics to collective states and transitions. Starting from uniformly random initial conditions, simulations reveal a rich phase diagram in the $(b,f_b)$ plane, comprising four collective states: spin-glass frustrated out-group favoritism, nondiscriminatory polarization, discrimination with opinion alignment, and discrimination without opinion alignment. Which state emerges depends on both the strength and prevalence of the bias. These results show how simple local learning dynamics can generate qualitatively distinct forms of polarization and discrimination, underscoring the need for population-level safety analysis of multi-agent systems. They also suggest measurable order parameters for characterizing analogous collective states in human societies.

entry.title: Gossip Agents: Reputation through Opinion Dynamics over Evolving Networks
entry.summary: Sustained cooperation among self-interested learning agents is essential in many shared environments. Reputation systems are among the best-studied mechanisms for promoting such cooperation. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches, however, typically assume that reputation is either globally available to all agents or derived solely from an agent's own observations, leaving largely unexplored how reputational information propagates between agents. We study gossip, the exchange of information about third parties, as a mechanism for reputation diffusion over dynamic communication networks. Agents form private opinions from limited observations and exchange them with their neighbors following DeGroot opinion dynamics, while the communication network changes as agents interact and move. A tunable broadcast radius controls the reach of information, spanning private reputation, local gossip, and globally shared reputation. We study this framework in two \(n\)-player social dilemmas with distinct network dynamics: a Prisoner's Dilemma with randomly resampled interaction groups and Harvest, where communication neighborhoods emerge from agents' movements. Our results show that the reach of reputational information shapes cooperation in both environments. Moreover, in Harvest, reputation diffusion increases environmental rewards and leads to more peaceful and sustainable behavior.

entry.title: Federation over Harness
entry.summary: Modern LLM-powered agents increasingly improve through experience sharing, where distributed agents distill local reasoning experience into reusable knowledge, such as a shared insight library. Existing approaches, however, still heavily rely on manually designed prompts and workflows that determine both how local agents extract useful reasoning traces and how a central/global agent aggregates them to obtain common patterns and insights. We propose Federation over Harness (FoH), a framework that automatically evolves the harness for both local and global components in this distributed multi-agent reasoning pipeline. A server agent evolves the client harness for task solving and self-reflection while, at the same time, evolving its own harness for aggregating distributed reflections, maintaining shared knowledge, and updating subsequent client harnesses. Importantly, FoH requires no extra validation signals, such as ground-truth labels or validation data, during evolution; it learns solely from self-generated reflections produced by distributed agents. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that FoH consistently improves over single-agent baselines with a fixed harness and with harness self-evolution by 53.57% and 29.76%.

entry.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
entry.summary: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. More details are available on our project page at https://guoweixu.com/mpt/.

entry.title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
entry.summary: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks. We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource. This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests. We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes forgoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements. We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings. Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or lightweight models. Alongside cooperation, we observe exclusionary coalitions and rare divide-and-conquer strategies. SCARCE provides a controlled setting for proactively and systematically auditing how these relationships emerge, shape access to resources, and affect the safety and coordination of multi-agent systems.
